fact: Veterinary behaviorists writing for VCA Animal Hospitals say any dog may dig to cool off on a very hot day, and some dogs dig because of the smell or sound of voles and moles underground.
quote: On a very hot summer day any dog may dig a hole to cool off. Breeds such as the terriers have been bred to flush out prey or dig for rodents. With their ability to hear high frequency sounds, and their highly acute sense of smell, some dogs dig as a direct result of odors or sounds such as those from voles and moles that attract the pet from beneath the ground.
source_label: VCA Animal Hospitals, Dogs and Destructive Digging (Debra Horwitz, DVM, and Gary Landsberg, DVM, veterinary behaviorists)
notes: Read in full with curl on 2026-09-25. The page carries an edit date of Jul 18, 2019.

fact: VCA's veterinary behaviorists say a dog digging after prey keeps digging until the prey is gone, a dog digging to cool off needs shade and water or to come inside on very hot days, and blocking all digging without dealing with the reason can lead to chewing, barking or escape attempts.
quote: Inhibiting or preventing all digging, without understanding and dealing with the dog's motivation could result in new behavior problems such as chewing, excessive vocalization, or escape behaviors. … For example, dogs that dig because they are pursuing prey will continue unless you can get rid of the prey. Dogs that dig in an attempt to get cool should be provided with a cool resting area with plenty of shade and water. On very hot days, it may be best to bring your dog inside.
source_label: VCA Animal Hospitals, Dogs and Destructive Digging (Debra Horwitz, DVM, and Gary Landsberg, DVM, veterinary behaviorists)

fact: VCA's veterinary behaviorists say covering a digging spot with a hard surface may teach a dog to leave that spot alone but does not stop it digging somewhere else, and that dogs also dig to escape confinement or from separation anxiety.
quote: Dogs also dig to escape from confinement or due to separation anxiety. … or covering the surface with one that is impervious (asphalt/patio stones) might teach the pet to avoid the digging site even in the owner's absence. These techniques do not however prevent the pet from digging in other locations. … Another alternative is to provide an area within the pen or run where digging is allowed.
source_label: VCA Animal Hospitals, Dogs and Destructive Digging (Debra Horwitz, DVM, and Gary Landsberg, DVM, veterinary behaviorists)

fact: Humane World for Animals says digging after burrowing animals tends to focus on one area, the roots of trees or shrubs, or a path; digging for comfort tends to sit near foundations, big shade trees or water; and a dog digging under or along a fence may be trying to escape.
quote: Dogs often dig in an effort to catch burrowing animals or insects who live in your yard. This may be the case if the digging is: Focused on a single area rather than the boundaries of the yard … At the roots of trees or shrubs … In a "path" layout … In hot weather, dogs may dig holes to lie in the cool dirt. … The holes are near the foundations of buildings, large shade trees or a water source. … Your dog may be digging to escape if they dig under or along a fence.
source_label: Humane World for Animals, How to get your dog to stop digging
notes: The prey signs are a bulleted list on the page; the ellipses mark list breaks and skipped text.

fact: Humane World for Animals says dogs left alone in the yard for long periods dig for entertainment, warns that anything that poisons wildlife can poison a dog too, and suggests a behavior professional when nothing else works.
quote: They're left alone in the yard for long periods of time without the company of their human family. … Anything that poisons wildlife can poison your dog too. … You may also want to consult a behavior professional for additional help.
source_label: Humane World for Animals, How to get your dog to stop digging

fact: For a dog that digs out under the fence, Humane World for Animals suggests chicken wire at the base of the fence with its sharp edges rolled away from the yard, large rocks partly buried along the fence line, burying the fence bottom 1 to 2 feet, or chain-link laid flat and anchored to the fence bottom.
quote: Bury chicken wire at the base of the fence. Be sure to roll the sharp edges away from your yard. Place large rocks, partially buried, along the bottom of the fence line. Bury the bottom of the fence 1 to 2 feet below the surface. Place chain-link fencing on the ground (anchored to the bottom of the fence) to make it uncomfortable for your dog to walk near the fence.
source_label: Humane World for Animals, How to get your dog to stop digging

fact: Humane World for Animals suggests giving a dedicated digger its own digging zone of loose soil or sand, or a child-sized sandbox.
quote: If your dog is a dedicated digger, set aside an area of the yard where it's OK for them to dig and teach them where that digging zone is: Cover the digging zone with loose soil or sand. Or use a child-sized sandbox.
source_label: Humane World for Animals, How to get your dog to stop digging

fact: Humane World for Animals describes an L-shaped wire footer along a fence, ideally buried about a foot deep and bent out at 90 degrees a foot or more, and says it can also be laid on the surface and covered.
quote: Ideally, these footers are buried about a foot deep and are extended out at a 90-degree angle a foot or more to present a horizontal barrier to any animal who decides to dig underneath the fence. … It is not absolutely necessary that the L-footer be buried. You can lay it on the surface if digging is made impossible by foundation plants, roots or rocky soil.
source_label: Humane World for Animals, How to stop animals from digging or burrowing under fences
notes: Written for keeping wildlife out; the footer is the same shape for a dog digging out.

fact: The American Kennel Club says dogs dig after rodents, dig shallow beds in cool earth on hot days (thick-coated Northern breeds especially), dig to get under barriers, and dig because it relieves boredom.
quote: Yards infested with rodents may have dogs digging intensively to find moles or mice. There are other practical reasons for digging as well. For example, dogs may dig a shallow bed in the cool earth to help beat the heat on a warm summer’s day. Thick-coated Northern breeds like the Alaskan Malamute or Siberian Husky may be especially prone to this. … Dogs also will dig to get under barriers. … Finally, dogs dig because it’s incredibly entertaining. It’s a great relief for bored dogs with nothing else to occupy their time.
source_label: American Kennel Club, Why Do Dogs Dig? Common Reasons and How to Manage the Behavior (Stephanie Gibeault, updated April 1, 2026)

fact: CSU Extension says voles stay active all year without hibernating, and most of their damage happens in winter, when they travel their grass runways under snow cover.
quote: Voles are active day and night throughout the year and do not hibernate. … Most damage occurs in the winter when voles move through their grass runways under the protection of snow.
source_label: CSU Extension Fact Sheet 6.507, Managing Voles in Colorado (published May 2025, reviewed August 2025)
notes: The old fact-sheet URL (/topic-areas/natural-resources/managing-voles-in-colorado-6-507/) 301-redirects here, and PlantTalk 2310 cites it as 6.507.

fact: CSU Extension places prairie voles in grasslands and along streams and irrigated land in eastern Colorado, and meadow voles along the South Platte River; voles live in heavy cover of grass and litter, and close fall mowing and clearing tall grass near lawns reduces their damage.
quote: Eight species of voles are found widely throughout various ecosystems of Colorado, in heavy ground cover of grasses, grass-like plants, and litter. … Meadow voles (Microtus pennsylvanicus) primarily occur from north to south central Colorado and along the South Platte River. … Prairie voles (Microtus ochrogaster) are found in grasslands and along streams and irrigated lands in eastern Colorado. … Damage to lawns can be reduced by close mowing in the fall before snow arrives and by mowing and removing tall grassy cover near lawns.
source_label: CSU Extension Fact Sheet 6.507, Managing Voles in Colorado (published May 2025, reviewed August 2025)

fact: CSU Extension lists vole signs as runways 1 to 2 inches wide through matted grass, burrows, and spongy soil.
quote: Other signs of damage by voles include 1) 1 to 2 inch-wide runways through matted grass and burrows; 2) visual sightings; 3) hawks circling overhead and diving into fields; and 4) spongy soil from burrowing activity.
source_label: CSU Extension Fact Sheet 6.507, Managing Voles in Colorado (published May 2025, reviewed August 2025)

fact: CSU Extension's PlantTalk Colorado says moles are rare in Colorado outside the far eastern plains, voles and pocket gophers are among the most common burrowers, and pocket gopher tunnels run 2.5 to 3.5 inches wide in the top 4 to 18 inches of soil, marked by soil mounds with no open hole.
quote: Moles are rarely found in Colorado, and only in the very eastern plains. If you are outside that area, the species causing damage is one of the other four. Voles and pocket gophers are amongst the most common. … The main signs of damage from pocket gophers include mounds of soil (with no apparent hole) … The tunnels are usually 2.5-3.5” in diameter, and are usually found in the top 4-18” of soil.
source_label: PlantTalk Colorado 2310, Difference between Voles damage and Pocket Gopher damage (CSU Extension)

fact: A pet-turf manufacturer says most turf is tufted, each blade a loop through the backing, so a dog can grab one end and pull it out.
quote: Most turf products are “tufted” which means the blade is just a loop through the backing. This leaves it vulnerable to a dog grabbing one end and pulling it out — and this is how dogs end up chewing on artificial grass.
source_label: K9Grass by ForeverLawn, Do pets chew dog friendly turf? (manufacturer FAQ)
notes: A manufacturer selling knitted-backing turf; copy attributes it as a manufacturer's statement, not a finding.

fact: The same manufacturer says turf held down only by spikes or the weight of its infill leaves edges a dog can pull up, and once pulled up, the blades and the spikes become things a dog can swallow.
quote: Installation must ensure all edges are firmly and safely secured. Dog friendly turf secured with spikes or weighted down with infill leaves the product edges vulnerable to dogs pulling up the product. Once pulled up, the grass as well as the spikes become components the dogs can devour.
source_label: K9Grass by ForeverLawn, Do pets chew dog friendly turf? (manufacturer FAQ)
notes: The page's next sentence gives a fastener spacing; this page leaves fastener specs to the nails-vs-staples guide, so it is not quoted.

fact: The manufacturer says blades a dog can pull out whole are a choking hazard that can encourage more digging, and advises buyers to ask for a sample and test it.
quote: K9Grass synthetic turf is designed to inhibit dogs from digging through it. Blades that can be pulled on one end and completely removed by a curious dog can be a choking hazard, and could end up provoking dogs to keep digging. … When in doubt about product design quality, we advise that you request a sample and test it.
source_label: K9Grass by ForeverLawn, Frequently Asked Questions (manufacturer FAQ)

fact: Firestone requires artificial turf to be anchored at all edges and seams and separated from other landscape areas by bender board, concrete curbing or a similar border.
quote: Artificial turf shall be anchored at all edges and seams. … Artificial turf shall be separated from other landscape areas by a bender board, concrete curbing or similar material to conceal edges of the turf.
source_label: Firestone Development Code 16.6.4.F.2.e.iv and e.vi (codified through Ord. No. 1072, Dec. 10, 2025)
notes: Read through the Municode API (api.municode.com CodesContent, jobId 488870, productId 18062) on 2026-09-25; the library page renders by script.

fact: Firestone requires at least a 3-foot buffer of permeable, living landscape between the edge of artificial turf and any property line.
quote: A minimum of three (3) foot buffer comprised of permeable surfaces with living and organic landscape material shall be required between the edge of the artificial turf and any property line.
source_label: Firestone Development Code 16.6.4.F.2.b.iii (codified through Ord. No. 1072, Dec. 10, 2025)
notes: Same clause as firestone-co.fdc-16.6.4-buffer-slope in layers/local; read again for this guide through the Municode API on 2026-09-25.

fact: Firestone's code says artificial turf may not have holes, tears, seam separations or uplifted surfaces, and damaged areas must be repaired or replaced to match the rest of the turf.
quote: Artificial turf areas shall not contain weeds, holes, tears, stains, discolorations, seam separations, uplifted surfaces, heat degradation, depressions, odors, excessive wear, or similar deformities and measures of deterioration. Damaged or worn areas shall be repaired or removed and replaced in manner that results in consistent appearance with the existing artificial turf.
source_label: Firestone Development Code 16.6.4.F.2.f.iii (codified through Ord. No. 1072, Dec. 10, 2025)
